episode_title: Hila Qu on Growth Accounting, PLG Funnel Math, and Structuring Growth Teams
guest_role: Former VP of Growth at GitLab and Acorns, Growth Advisor
topic: Growth Accounting, PLG Metrics, Growth Equations, Cohort Retention, WAU/MAU
summary: Hila Qu breaks down the mathematical foundations of growth: the growth accounting equation, diagnosing active user leakage, WAU/MAU ratios, and how to organize growth engineering squads around core metrics.
key_takeaways: Growth Accounting Equation: Active Users(t) = New + Retained + Resurrected - Churned.
Resurrection is often the most neglected growth lever for mature products with large inactive user databases.
Growth teams should be structured around stages of the user journey (Acquisition squad, Activation squad, Monetization squad) rather than technical layers.
A product's North Star metric must be broken down into an input tree of actionable sub-metrics owned by individual squads.

transcript.speaker: Lenny Rachitsky
transcript.text: Welcome to Lenny's Podcast. Today my guest is Hila Qu. Hila was the VP of Growth at GitLab and Acorns and is renowned for her rigorous, mathematical approach to product growth and growth accounting. Hila, welcome!

transcript.speaker: Hila Qu
transcript.text: Thank you Lenny, excited to dive into the math and organizational design behind growth.

transcript.speaker: Lenny Rachitsky
transcript.text: What is Growth Accounting, and why should every product team maintain a growth accounting dashboard?

transcript.speaker: Hila Qu
transcript.text: Growth Accounting is the balance sheet of your user base. The formula is simple: Your active users this period equal New Users plus Retained Users from last period plus Resurrected Users minus Churned Users. When your Monthly Active Users (MAU) goes up by 10,000, you might celebrate. But Growth Accounting reveals whether that growth was driven by 20,000 new users while 10,000 existing users secretly churned. If churn exceeds retention, you are inflating a dying balloon.

transcript.speaker: Lenny Rachitsky
transcript.text: Why do mature products under-invest in resurrection, and what tactics actually bring back dormant users?

transcript.speaker: Hila Qu
transcript.text: When a company is 3–5 years old, their dormant user database is often 10x larger than their monthly new signups. Bringing back a dormant user with high brand awareness is often 5x cheaper than acquiring a cold user through Google Ads. But resurrection fails when you send generic 'We miss you!' emails. Resurrection succeeds when triggered by relevant external context: a colleague shared a project, a major feature was released that solves their past blocker, or an automated summary of missed activity is delivered.

transcript.speaker: Lenny Rachitsky
transcript.text: How should leadership structure growth engineering teams?

transcript.speaker: Hila Qu
transcript.text: Structure growth pods by user journey phase rather than surface area. You have: 1. Acquisition/SEO pod (owns signup volume and CAC), 2. Activation pod (owns time-to-value and day-7 retention), 3. Monetization/Pricing pod (owns free-to-paid conversion and upgrade loops), and 4. Retention/Expansion pod (owns expansion ARR and resurrection). Each squad has its own PM, designer, full-stack engineers, and dedicated data analyst.

transcript.speaker: Lenny Rachitsky
transcript.text: What is the Quick Ratio in SaaS growth, and what is a healthy benchmark?

transcript.speaker: Hila Qu
transcript.text: The Quick Ratio measures user growth velocity against churn. The formula is: Quick Ratio = (New Users + Resurrected Users) / Churned Users. If your Quick Ratio is below 1.0, your user base is shrinking. If it is between 1.5 and 2.0, you have modest growth. If your Quick Ratio is 4.0+, you have top-quartile venture-scale growth efficiency.
